newsitem.title: DUBAI: RTRS - Saudi imports of Australian live sheep may resume.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Saudi imports of Australian live sheep may resume.

text.p: Leading livestock importer Saudi Arabia plans to build two quarantine units for imported sheep, which could pave the way for a resumption of Australian sheep exports to the kingdom, industry executives said on Sunday.
"Saudi Arabia is establishing two quarantine zones in Jeddah and this will give the Australians a chance to resume sheep exports to the kingdom," a Saudi industry source said.
"When they are established, this will mean the kingdom will be able to have more sources of sheep and imports from all over the world will increase," he added by telephone from Jeddah.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world's most lucrative livestock markets, imports about two million sheep each year, but exporters to the kingdom face stringent health requirements, the industry source added.

The Saudi newspaper al-Eqtisadiah on Sunday reported the kingdom had rejected 10,000 head of sheep in the last three weeks that failed to meet health requirements and was building the two quarantine units in Jeddah.
Australia, the world's largest exporter of live sheep, in March suspended efforts to resume its livestock trade with Saudi Arabia until exporters could meet the kingdom's regulations.

The decision dealt a serious blow to Australia's drive to revive its biggest world market for livestock, which was worth around $130 million annually before it lost the business in 1991 when the kingdom rejected several shiploads on health grounds.
Last year, a ship carrying 75,000 Australian sheep worth $3.5 million, the first shipment in four years, was diverted to Jordan due to fears the animals would fail a health inspection.

An industry source said on Sunday the quarantine units under construction at the Jeddah Islamic Port and the Khomra area in south Jeddah would significantly reduce the chances of the kingdom rejecting sheep.

"It is much too expensive for exporters to maintain efforts to export to the kingdom after their livestock has been rejected. The quarantine units will help," he said. Imported sheep would be held in the units for 21 days, during which time they would be checked for disease before being allowed to enter the kingdom, the paper said.
Industry sources said there had been no new negotiations between Saudi Arabia and Australian exporters since the ship was diverted to Jordan.
